author: maxime-leroy
body:
The check compared the API headers with the parent commit, which required a GR_API_VERSION bump from every commit changing a type, including a commit changing a type another commit of the same series had just introduced. Nothing outside the series ever saw that intermediate layout, and bumping for it puts clients and daemons in lockstep for something which never shipped.

GR_API_VERSION is negotiated in the hello handshake between two binaries, so what it has to describe is the compatibility of released versions. Compare against the last release tag instead, which needs one bump per release cycle at most and leaves the commit layout of a series free.

What this gives up is the mixing of binaries built from two different commits of the same cycle: they announce the same version while the API has changed in between. PREV_REVISION is still honoured for anyone wanting the previous behaviour.

author: xarmian
body:
Fixes BUG-2725. Built by Rook (docapp seat 2) under Dave's day-49 ruling and the lead's plan-A conditions.

## The defect

`deliveredSessionCount` applied three of `watchNotificationVisible`'s four gates. The missing one is the first thing delivery checks: `vis.allows(CollectionID, ItemID)`.

- **Broadcast** over-reported — it counted sessions whose stream drops the notification.
- **Targeted** was worse. The publish-skip reads this count, so the gate passed, the push went out, the stream dropped it on visibility, and the response said `delivered_sessions: 1`. An instruction lost behind a success.

No payload ever leaked; `vis.allows` was doing its job. The count was the liar.

## The fix

Visibility is **re-resolved at push time**, not snapshotted — Dave's ruling, for the reason `watchNotificationVisible` re-reads per notification: membership and grants are revocable, so a value cached at connect goes wrong exactly when revocation is what makes it matter.

The one input that cannot be re-resolved is the target connection's **auth transport**. `computeWatchAccessVisibility` consults `isBearerAuth` exactly once, inside the admin bypass, and the pushing request only knows its own transport. So `SessionOrigin.BearerAuth` is recorded at `Add()` from the request that opens the stream.

**That is not the snapshot the ruling rejected**, and the distinction is the load-bearing part of this PR: auth transport is a property of the connection, fixed when it opened and not revocable while it is held, so it cannot go stale. `Armed` is the standing precedent. Both the field and `SessionOrigin` carry the rule for future extenders — *connection properties are admissible, derived authorization state never is.*

`SessionOrigin` is a separate type from `SessionIdentity` rather than a field on it, because `SessionIdentity` documents itself as self-declared and never verified; folding a server-derived, security-relevant fact in there would silently retract that warning for one field.

`computeWatchAccessVisibility` now takes a `bool` instead of an `*http.Request` — which is what makes the per-connection input visible in the signature and lets the count answer for a connection it is not serving.

## The cost objection is retired structurally, not argued

"Re-resolve per counted session" reads like N access checks per push. It is **at most two**, and `sessionVisibility`'s memo makes that true by construction rather than by careful calling.

The enumeration is in the code as a receipt: every input to `computeWatchAccessVisibility` — platform role, workspace membership, `CollectionAccess`, `GuestVisibleResources`, `GetMemberCollectionAccess`, `ListSystemCollectionIDs` — is per-USER and identical across the one user's sessions this function counts. `bearerAuth` is the sole varying input. One varying boolean bounds the answers at two, and `TestPushSessionVisibility_ResolvesAtMostTwice` pins it with 50 sessions so the bound is verifiable rather than claimed.

## How the defect is reproduced

Over-counting needs the pusher able to push while one of their OWN sessions cannot see the item. Per-user narrowing cannot produce that — it resolves identically for every stream that user holds. So the reproducible case is the per-connection one: a **platform admin who is not a member of the target workspace**, pushing over a **cookie** (that bypass is cookie-only), holding an armed **bearer**-opened stream.

## Tests

Ten, each with a control leg or an asserted premise:

| test | asserts |
|---|---|
| `BroadcastDoesNotCountSessionsDeliveryWillDrop` | the over-count is 0 |
| `BroadcastStillCountsVisibleSessions` | control — flips ONLY transport, requires 1 |
| `TargetedAtInvisibleSessionSkipsPublish` | the publish is SKIPPED, observed on the bus |
| `TargetedAtVisibleSessionPublishes` | control — a visible target still publishes |
| `ResolvesAtMostTwice` | the ≤2 bound, 50 sessions, counting resolver |
| `HandlerPassesRealVisibility` | CONVE-19 wiring — nil vs real visibility differ |
| `CountAgreesWithWhatTheStreamReceives` | end-to-end count↔delivery symmetry, real stream |
| `MissingUserIsNotVisible` | an absent user is not-visible, and is NOT an error |
| `PropagatesVisibilityError` | an unreadable store surfaces as an error, not as 0 |
| `ComputeWatchAccessVisibility_ReportsStoreFailure` | the resolver reports failures; deny-everything alongside |

`TargetedAtInvisibleSessionSkipsPublish` watches the **bus**, not the response, because `handlePushToItem` sets `pushed:true` on both branches — the response cannot distinguish them. Per CONVE-12 it asserts what the wrong behaviour would leave behind.

The fixtures assert their own premises (first user really is a platform admin; that admin is really not a member). If either stopped holding, both transports would resolve full access and every assertion would pass for a reason unrelated to the fix.

## Mutation matrix (first pass — superseded by the final matrix below)

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | drop the visibility filter from the count | caught (5) |
| M2 | handler passes nil visibility (fixed but unwired) | caught (4) |
| M3 | `allows()` hardwired true | caught (6) |
| M4 | `allows()` hardwired false | caught (9) |
| M5 | memo removed, resolve every call | caught (1) |
| M6 | `Add` ignores origin | caught (5) |
| M7 | admin bypass reads transport inverted | caught (5) |
| M8 | resolver fails OPEN on unresolvable user | caught (1) |
| M9 | stream reads a constant transport, not its own | caught (1) |

**M5's first version was a false catch** and is recorded as such: it left `i` declared-and-unused, so the "failure" was a build error rather than a detection. Rebuilt to replace the whole body, it compiles and is caught by exactly the one test that should catch it. A mutation that fails to compile measures nothing.

**M8 and M9 survived this first pass.** Both are closed by the two tests in the second commit — which is why those tests exist at all. The counts in this table are from that pass; the authoritative final matrix (11 applied, 10 caught, 1 recorded survivor) is in the codex section below.

## What this does NOT fix, stated rather than implied

The **under-count**. A stream past `maxSessionsPerUser` receives broadcasts while never entering the registry, so it is invisible here however exactly the predicate is reproduced. `delivered_sessions` remains an **estimate with error in both directions**, and every consumer-facing description already says so. Dave's ruling scoped this unit to the over-side; the lead ratified that scoping.

**Search boundary:** the predicate was traced through `internal/server` only — `handlers_push.go`, `handlers_watch_events.go`, `handlers_watch_access.go`, `session_presence*.go`. `internal/watchevents` was not swept for other consumers of this predicate shape.

## Also lands: the BUG-2752 refutation sentinel

BUG-2752 (filed and refuted during this unit's recon) claimed the OAuth workspace allow-list went unenforced on `/api/v1/events/stream`. author: hardcode83
body:
Tres bloques, un commit cada uno. Salen de dos fricciones reales medidas en sesiones con varias features en paralelo y una sesión por feature (workspaces de Orca, que **son** worktrees enlazados del repo: `git-common-dir` apunta al clon principal).

## 1. `fix(retire)` — decomisionar desde dentro del propio worktree

`/sdd:archive` nunca retiraba el worktree «de primeras», por dos causas que eran del **llamante**, no del worktree:

- **«estás dentro» era un bloqueo.** Con una sesión por feature, la sesión que archiva *es* la que está dentro, así que el worktree no lo retiraba nunca la ejecución que había terminado su trabajo. Comprobado contra git real: `git worktree remove` sí funciona desde dentro; lo que se rompe es todo lo posterior (`git branch -d`, binding, ACL `deny delete`, registro de plugins), que corre con un cwd que ya no resuelve y falla con `Unable to read current working directory` mientras el retiro se declara hecho. Ahora `retire` se muda al worktree principal antes de tocar git y lo reporta (`self_retired`, `relocated_to`).
- **El `teardown:` no declarado** sigue siendo una negativa (adivinar `down --volumes` sobre la BD de alguien no es del toolkit, regla 9), pero la línea a declarar se **deriva** de lo que reportó docker (`--rmi local` incluido si hay imágenes construidas; sin proyecto compose no se sugiere nada). La imprimen `worktrees` y `residue`, y la pregunta de cierre de `/sdd:archive` la lleva ya escrita.

## 2. `feat(ship)` — sincronizar la base antes de abrir el PR

«Esta rama tiene conflictos» era un tramo sin dueño: review ya terminó, archive se niega a empezar antes del merge. Ahora `sync-base` corre en cada ship (no-op si la base no se movió):

- **Merge y nunca rebase**: un rebase reescribiría `implementation_sha`, el ancla que lee el gate de merge (regla 8).
- Une `sdd/roadmap.md` y `sdd/metrics.md` con `git merge-file --union` — más la comprobación de que **no duplica** entradas, que es lo que mantiene honesto el camino automático.
- Cualquier otro conflicto sale con **exit 2** y el merge en curso: lo resuelve ship, vuelve a pasar la verificación **declarada por el proyecto** y lo registra con `record-sync`. Si falla (`--failed`), no se abre PR: `BLOCKED.md` y a `/sdd:review`.
- `validate-ship` pasa a `--first-parent` y autoriza dos formas de commit; `verify_equivalent_merge` mide el límite contra la punta de la rama, porque con un sync por medio el punto de rama viejo habría roto la evidencia `equivalent` de los merges por squash.

## 3. `feat(archive)` — integrar una base que avanzó al publicar

El commit de archive es el único que el flujo hace sobre la base, así que dos archives en paralelo divergen por construcción y chocan en los ficheros append-only. `publish-archive` los rebasa y resuelve por unión; lo que no puede decidir **restaura la rama intacta y se niega**. Sube la versión a 0.38.0.

## Verificación

- **329 tests** (`python3 -m unittest discover`) + los 4 validadores + release-guard, verde **en cada uno de los tres commits** por separado (311 / 324 / 329).
- **End-to-end por CLI en repos reales**, no con stubs: self-retire desde dentro (directorio y rama borrados, exit 0, instrucción de reubicación); sync con conflicto mixto (roadmap unido → `app.py` pendiente → negativa sin resolver → negativa con marcadores → `record-sync` con trailers → `validate-ship` verde con el ancla aún ancestro de HEAD); e integración de `publish-archive` contra un remoto bare de verdad.

## Límites conocidos

- El self-retire **no** libera a archive de estar en la rama base para escribir specs/roadmap/metrics, y git solo permite un worktree por rama: el paso 0 ahora te dice que pares antes de escribir en vez de dejar medio archive en la rama equivocada.
- La sugerencia de `teardown:` solo cubre compose. Un contenedor sin proyecto compose sigue negándose sin sugerencia, a propósito.
- No hay check nuevo en `/sdd:doctor`: «residuo sin teardown» es estado de máquina y los fixtures de doctor son árboles committeados — la superficie es `worktrees`/`residue`, que doctor ya ejecuta.

author: bechsteindigital
body:
Addresses #344.

## The gap

Everything the host records is an **aggregate** — `BackgroundJobTelemetry`, `PluginLifecycleTelemetry`, `WebhookTelemetry`, `PluginLifecycleSloEvaluator`. Those answer *is the platform healthy*.

None answers the question an operator actually asks: **this request took four seconds, who spent it?** Under ADR-013 several plugins from different repositories share one process and one database connection, so nothing about a query says who issued it. A plugin author debugging their own N+1 had no way to see it short of attaching a profiler to the whole host.

## Attribution is the hard half

Walking the stack would be expensive and unreliable across an `await`, so the host marks the scope where it hands control to a plugin. Those points are known and few — a plugin HTTP route, a job whose handler a plugin owns, a business event delivered to a plugin listener — and each already resolves the owning plugin for the availability gate, so the marking costs a lookup nobody had to add.

`PluginExecutionScope` is an `AsyncLocal` that **restores** the previous value rather than clearing it: a plugin calling another plugin's exported service must not leave the first credited with the second's queries.

Two rules that fall out of it, both tested:

- **Host work is attributed to nobody**, not to whatever ran before it. An attribution that guesses is worse than none — it names a culprit confidently and wrongly.
- **On HTTP the scope starts late**, after authentication, permission and availability. Those are the host's own work.

The test that matters most is the concurrent one: a shared process serves several plugins at once, and attribution that bleeds across requests would point at the wrong plugin with full confidence.

## It switches itself off

Off by default, and there is deliberately no way to enable it indefinitely: 10-minute ceiling, 500-command ring. The failure mode of a diagnostic tool is not being wrong — it is being switched on during an incident and forgotten.

Expiry is evaluated **on read** rather than by a timer. A timer would have to be disposed, and a recorder holding a live callback past its window is precisely what this is meant to avoid. A window beyond the ceiling is **clamped, not refused**; refusing only teaches callers to ask for the maximum every time, and the start response returns the *effective* window so an operator knows how long they actually have.

## Where the interceptor sits

On the host context **and** on `NpgsqlPluginDbContextProvider` — the single place a plugin `DbContext` is configured. Without the second, exactly the work this exists for would be invisible to a host-side interceptor.

Registered unconditionally even though the recorder is off: a switch that only takes effect after a restart is no use in the moment you need it. The idle cost is a field read and an early return.

## A rule I broke first

I built the endpoints from `JobEndpoints` as a model, and `ArchitectureRulesTests` caught it: minimal-API files are a **migration baseline that may only shrink**, and new endpoints are controllers. `JobEndpoints` is inventory, not example. Rewritten as `RecorderController`.

## Security

`diagnostics.record` is a permission of its own, not part of `job.read`. A recording contains **SQL command text**, including literals EF Core inlines into the statement — a wider disclosure than any other monitoring endpoint makes. Folding it into an existing key would have granted it to everyone who may watch the platform rather than to the people who debug it. Documented as such on both pages.

## Scope

Built: the recorder, attribution, the EF interceptor, the operator API, docs and gates.

**Not built**, and named here rather than left implicit: the Admin SPA view, the business-event timeline, and any CPU profiling. #344 lists all three. The question this was built for is *which plugin*, and in a shared process the database is where contention actually happens — the rest can follow once this is proven in use.

## Verification

```
dotnet test Callora.Host.sln -p:SkipAdminFrontend=true --filter "Category!=Slow"
Bestanden!  Fehler: 0, erfolgreich: 1627, gesamt: 1627
Bestanden!  Fehler: 0, erfolgreich:   34, gesamt:   34   (Analyzers)

cd docs-site && npm run lint
markdownlint  Summary: 0 issues in 0 files
cspell        Files checked: 72, Issues found: 0 in 0 files
```

1603 before, 1627 after — 24 new tests, each watched failing for the intended reason first.

Refs #344

body:
## Contexto

Primeira fatia da **Fase 2** (Design system) da trilha Robustez do Frontend. A auditoria pintou "561 hex / 2 SSOTs de cor" como problema grande — mas a **medição real** conta outra história:

- O SSOT de cor de marca (`BRAND_COLORS` em `ThemeContext`) **já existe** e é aplicado via `ConfigProvider` do AntD.
- O 2º SSOT morto (`constants/styles.ts`) **já foi deletado** (#1808).
- Dos ~194 hex de produção, **só 2** hardcodam a cor de **marca**. O resto são paletas de **chart/mapa/status/genéricas** — hardcode legítimo, não violação.

Então a alavanca aqui não é um codemod de massa (risco alto, ROI baixo) — é **fechar os 2 leaks e travar a regressão**.

## O que muda

1. **Corrige os 2 leaks** (passam a usar o token):
   - `HomePage.tsx` — `#004B3D` → `BRAND_COLORS.primaryDark`
   - `AppHeader.tsx` — `#006B52` → `BRAND_COLORS.primary`
2. **Guard `check-brand-colors.mjs`** + step no `frontend-ci` (ao lado do `check:ts-only`): falha o CI se algum componente hardcodar um dos 3 verdes distintos da marca (`#006B52`/`#004B3D`/`#E5EDE5`) fora do SSOT. Escopo **cirúrgico** — não toca paletas de chart/mapa/status.

## Por que não o codemod dos 561 hex

Medido: só 2 são violação real de marca. Os demais são cores de dados (choropleth do mapa, séries de dashboard, status AntD) onde o hex é intencional. Um codemod de massa arriscaria trocar cor onde a variante era proposital, pra ~zero ganho de consistência de marca. O guard já **estanca o sangramento** (zero-novos) sem esse risco.

## Frontend prototype — complete Moreland family-tree flow

Fixes the homepage/public Moreland viewer autoplay getting trapped between Malik Moreland and Elias + Clara Moreland.

### Root cause

The canonical demo path contains intentional repeated routing states. Malik appears twice and the parent household appears three times as the tour moves between branches. Autoplay used Array.indexOf(currentState), which always selected the first occurrence and restarted the Malik/parents loop.

### Correction

- Track the exact autoplay sequence position instead of searching for the first matching state.
- Preserve the correct position across repeated routing nodes.
- Align manual graph and path-list navigation with the nearest valid sequence step.
- Highlight only the active occurrence in the guided path.
- Cache-bust the viewer script so the frontend receives the correction after deployment.
- Add a Chromium regression that verifies the complete 11-step tour:
  1. Malik

body:
## Summary
- load the Hermes dashboard session token from durable Hermes config
- forward the restored token through the Fetch reverse tunnel after restarts and updates
- cover persisted-token recovery when the token is absent from the process environment

## Why
Hermes can load ~/.hermes/.env without exporting its values into the plugin process. The Fetch tunnel previously read only os.environ, so protected dashboard requests were forwarded without a token and returned 401 after some restart and update paths.

## Validation
- 468 passed, 1 skipped

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches dashboard session-token handling on the reverse tunnel, which gates protected requests. The change is small and uses the existing config loader, but a bad token path would still yield 401s or unauthenticated forwarding.
> 
> **Overview**
> Stops the Fetch reverse tunnel from forwarding protected dashboard requests without a session token after Hermes restarts or updates.
> 
> `AgentTunnel` now loads `HERMES_DASHBOARD_SESSION_TOKEN` via `_relay._config_value`, which falls back to `~/.hermes/.env` when the value is not exported into the plugin process. A regression test covers persisted-token recovery with an empty process environment.

author: soradozere
body:
Four follow-ups to the Impact board merged in #179, all from Sora reading the live board and pushing back. Two were his catches; two were mine being wrong.

## 1. Assists are not a double-count — question resolved

The Open Questions panel listed this as a possible bug: assists correlate **0.95** with returns per minute, are priced separately, and sit in the same job.

Checked, and it's not. An assist is a **capture** assist:

| | |
|---|---|
| my assists vs **my own** captures | **r = −0.21** (negative) |
| my assists vs **my teammates'** captures | r = +0.46 |
| team assists vs team captures | **r = 0.83** (~1.25 per capture) |
| team assists vs team returns | r = 0.44 |

You helped someone else score — hence negative against your own caps. Returners collect most of them because they're mid-map making it happen; that co-occurrence is where the 0.95 came from.

They're also load-bearing: removing them collapses the returner group (6.3 → 5.1) and takes the role gap from 19% to 33%. **No scoring change** — the panel section is rewritten from "a possible bug" to "resolved", since it's public and was advertising a defect that doesn't exist.

## 2. Returns were genuinely under-priced

Sora spotted a returner main sitting well below the cappers. Real: the returner group's median sat **14% below** cap and base, because the constrained tuner couldn't lift it further without breaking his stat ordering.

Multiplying the Return job by 1.3 costs nothing measurable:

| | Reliability | Role gap | Returner median |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 0.83 | 15% | 14% low |
| **after** | 0.83 | 15% | **4% low** |

Ordering still holds — capture 24.6% of the board, return 21.8%, BC kill 14.5%, mine grab 13.9%.

## 3. Strength of schedule

Sora: a player whose lobbies are consistently weaker is flattered. True and measurable — ben faces the weakest opposition of all 32 players (7.65 vs a pool average of 8.11), worth ~5% of his production.

Production responds at **−1.021 points per point of opponent strength**, measured *within* players so it isn't just "good players meet good players", across a per-match opponent-strength spread of sd 0.507.

Opponent strength is the other side's usual production, computed **leave-one-out** so a big game can't inflate the rating it's judged against. Spread across the four jobs proportionally (jobs still sum to the value, all stay non-negative), clamped to [0.5×, 1.5×].

Applied at **1× the measured slope**. Reliability is flat at every strength tested (0.826 / 0.827 / 0.824 / 0.827 for none / 1× / 2× / 3×), so there's no evidence for more and more would be an invented number. **The slope cannot speak to lobbies outside the observed range** — whether a player would be decimated in a genuinely elite lobby is beyond this data.

I initially argued for leaving this out on the grounds that it "adds noise". That was asserted, not tested; when tested it's free, and free-and-correct wins.

## 4. A dash instead of a number for jobs not played

Sora read vee's Support column as a deduction for never playing support. It isn't — doing none of a job scores exactly zero — but the column is standardised, so a number under 50 reads as a mark against you.

The counterfactual confirms there's nothing wrong with the scoring: giving vee pool-average support moves him **15th → 15th**. Support is 6% of a typical rating. What costs him is being near-zero at cap and base (60% of a rating between them).

So it's a display problem. Below 30% of a job's pool average, the column now shows a dash with a tooltip saying it costs nothing.

## Notes

- **156 tests passing** (33 on this lib, up from 31). Typecheck clean for changed files.
- One existing test asserted a role-swapper gets *exactly* half of each specialist's contribution. No longer true to 10 decimals now that the three face different opposition — asserted within 10% instead, which is the real invariant, plus two new tests for the adjustment's own guarantees.
- Verified live against August data throughout.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)


---

## Added after review

**Merged main.** The PR went `CONFLICTING` when main moved on (#180, #163) — the three Impact files came back as `add/add`, which is squash-merge fallout: #179 created them on main, but this branch's history doesn't contain that squash commit, so git saw both sides as independently adding the same paths. Verified nothing on main had touched any of the three since #179 (byte-identical to the 3b1fda2 snapshot) before taking this branch's copies. `reports-tab.tsx` auto-merged cleanly.

**Rewrote "How it works"** as a plain-language explainer — one sentence, four steps, the price table, the two rules that make it fair, what's deliberately ignored, and what the board can and cannot claim. The previous copy explained the four jobs and the calibration, which answered a question nobody was asking; this answers "how do I get a higher number".

**Naming.** Comments and PR bodies referred to the site owner by real name. All replaced with Sora, and a `commit-msg` / `pre-commit` hook pair now blocks it at the git level for every session and worktree on the clone.

**Matched the board's styling to the other three.** It was the only leaderboard on the Stats tab rendering as a bare table on the page background. Now uses the same wrapper as Wins, ELO and TrueSkill — surface tint, border, rounded, header strip above a divider — with the colour legend and qualifying line moved into that strip. The board name isn't repeated inside the box the way "Wins Leaderboard" is, since it already sits above with the experimental badge. Loading and empty states take the box too.

author: rainer-friederich
body:
<!-- mysticat-pr-skill -->

## 1. Abstract

Adds project **pause / resume** to the Semrush Project Engine client: the two endpoints Semrush shipped for the weekly-workspace data migration, exposed as `pauseProject` / `resumeProject` on the typed transport and modelled in the stateful mock.

## 2. Reasoning

Semrush is re-shaping AIO projects into weekly-cadence workspaces. Before the ClickHouse data can be moved, every old workspace has to stop writing — otherwise the migration reads and writes the same rows and the data is corrupted. Pausing is the mechanism they built for that: it releases a project's prompt limits and stops data collection while configuration and historical data are preserved, so to a customer it looks like a switch to weekly cadence rather than an outage. It is also the rollback lever — if the migration goes wrong, the old projects are resumed.

Semrush delivered the two endpoints as a swagger delta on 2026-08-24. The client had no way to call them, so the bulk pause that gates the migration could not be driven from our side.

## 3. High-level overview of the changes

**Before:** the Project Engine client had no notion of a paused project — no way to pause or resume one, and no way to read whether one is paused.

**After:** both actions are first-class transport methods, and the paused state is readable off any project.

- The vendored swagger gains the two delivered paths (`POST .../projects/{project_id}/pause` and `.../resume`), spliced in verbatim and re-locked. The delivered YAML is a delta — only the paths a release added — so it is spliced rather than dropped in wholesale; the README's "Spec source" section now documents that procedure and the deep-compare that evidences it.
- Two overlay corrections fill what the delta left out. **CR23** adds `is_paused` to `model.ProjectResponse` — Semrush ships the field on every project read but never documented it, so the generated type previously had no way to express whether a project is paused. **CR24** declares the `404` both actions return for an unknown project id.
- The transport facade gains `pauseProject` / `resumeProject` (32 → 34 in-spec operations).
- The mock serves both routes over a pure decision table, with `is_paused` on the project read-view.

The behaviour the mock reproduces, and that a caller should expect:

| call | response |
| --- | --- |
| pause a running project | `202`, empty body |
| pause an already-paused project | `202` — **idempotent** |
| resume a paused project | `202`, empty body |
| resume a project that is not paused | `409 {"message":"project is not paused"}` |
| either, on an unknown project id | `404 {"message":"not found"}` |

The asymmetry is the operationally significant part: **a bulk pause is safely re-runnable, a bulk resume is not.** Anything driving the migration has to track what it paused, or tolerate 409s on the way back.

Neither action touches `publish_status`, `is_draft`, `published_at` or `updated_at` — a paused project still reads `publish_status: live`.

## 4. Required information

- Other: Semrush announcement of the endpoints + the delivered swagger — https://semrush.slack.com/archives/C0B02FWQYBF/p1785486744709569

## 6. Affected / used mysticat-workspace projects

- **mysticat-data-service** — contract, no code dependency. Its `scripts/serenity_migration` CLI is what actually drives the bulk pause for the migration, against the same two endpoints via its own Python client rather than this one. The two implementations have to agree on the semantics, which is why the probe findings in section 7 are recorded here rather than only in the mock.
- **spacecat-api-service** — consumed / contract. Pins `@adobe/spacecat-shared-project-engine-client` (currently `1.18.1`) for its serenity transport, and pulls the client's published GHCR mock image in `test/it/postgres/docker-compose.yml`. Nothing breaks on this PR: the transport additions are purely additive. On its next version bump it picks up the two new methods and the `is_paused` field, and the refreshed mock image.

## 7. Additional information outside the code

Every behaviour claim above was probed against **prod** on 2026-08-24, not inferred from the swagger — which matters here, because the swagger was wrong twice.

Probed on the LLMO-Dev-2 scaffolding workspace `0a496c87-84c6-4b06-9201-da642950820f` ("Brand-A"), project `997e17c3-…` ("CH-de"), which was returned to its original running state afterwards. Two findings contradicted the delivered spec:

- **Pause is idempotent.** The swagger declares `409` on both actions; live returns a second `202` for pausing an already-paused project. Only `resume` uses the `409`, with `{"message":"project is not paused"}`.
- **`is_paused` exists and is undocumented.** It is present on the v1 detail, the v1 list and the v2 list. Without CR23 there would be no way to ask the API which projects are paused — which the migration's rollback path depends on.

Also worth knowing for anyone consuming these: **error bodies are JSON but served as `content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`.** This is systemic on this API rather than new (`publish`'s 404 does the same), but the consequence for an `openapi-fetch` caller is that `error` arrives as a raw string, not a parsed object — so `error.message` is `undefined` against live even though it works against the mock, which serves `application/json` like every other mock handler.

One claim could not be verified: the swagger states resume is "subject to the same quota check as publishing". Exercising that needs a project inside a zero-allocation workspace, which cannot be created there in the first place. The mock models the `405` but checks it last, after both live-verified branches, so the unverified rule can never pre-empt an observed one.

## 8. Test plan

**Done locally:** the mock e2e suite drives the two new routes end to end against a running Counterfact server — the full branch table above, plus `is_paused` visibility on the detail and list reads and the quota interaction on resume. The live prod probe is described in section 7.

**Verifying against Semrush prod** (no dev/stage environment exists for the Project Engine — it is a single live Semrush API):

- Pick a disposable project in an LLMO-Dev-2 scaffolding workspace, e.g. `0a496c87-84c6-4b06-9201-da642950820f`.
- `POST /v1/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{project}/pause` with an IMS bearer → expect `202` and `content-length: 0`.
- Re-read the project (`GET /v1/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{project}?draft=true`) → expect `is_paused: true`, `publish_status` unchanged.
- `POST .../resume` → `202`; re-read → `is_paused: false`. A second `resume` → `409`.
- Leave the project running.

**Consumers:** nothing to verify on `spacecat-api-service` until it bumps the dependency — this PR does not change any operation it currently calls.

author: digiserg
body:
Fixes #198.

## Problem

In `axonops/charts/axon-server/templates/statefulset.yaml`, the `containers:` key was inside the `{{- if and .Values.persistence.enabled .Values.persistence.enableInitChown }}` block that guards the `fsgroup-volume` init container. With either value `false`, the key was never rendered and the `axon-server` container was emitted as the last item under `initContainers:`. The pod spec then had no `containers:` at all and the API server rejected the manifest with `spec.containers: Required value`, so the release failed to install — no StatefulSet was created and no pod was ever scheduled.

`initContainers:` was also emitted unconditionally, rendering as a bare key with no items whenever the guard was false.

Both values default to `true`, so a default install was never affected. Ephemeral or CI installs with `persistence.enabled=false`, and installs that disable only the init chown because the storage class already sets ownership or because the cluster's Pod Security Standards forbid its `runAsUser: 0`, hit it.

## Change

`containers:` moves outside the conditional and `initContainers:` moves inside it — the shape `axondb-search/templates/statefulset.yaml` and `axondb-timeseries/templates/sts.yaml` already use.

Chart version and the umbrella chart's dependency pin go `2.1.14` → `2.1.16`. `2.1.15` is skipped because the CI appVersion bump (`2db452f`, on `main` only) already published it.

## Verification

All four value combinations render a `containers:` list holding `axon-server`, and `initContainers:` only when there is an init container to put under it:

| `persistence.enabled` | `enableInitChown` | `containers` | `initContainers` |
|---|---|---|---|
| true | true | `[axon-server]` | `[fsgroup-volume]` |
| true | false | `[axon-server]` | absent |
| false | true | `[axon-server]` | absent |
| false | false | `[axon-server]` | absent |

- `helm template` with default values is byte-identical before and after, so existing installs are unaffected.
- `helm lint` passes.
- Server-side `kubectl apply --dry-run` was not run: no authenticated cluster was available in this environment (`gke-gcloud-auth-plugin` failed). Validation was done by parsing the rendered YAML and asserting the pod spec structure directly, which covers the missing-`containers` failure this fixes.

`CHANGELOG.md` updated under `[Unreleased] / Fixed`.

body:
Closes #88

**도메인이 살았습니다.**

| | |
|---|---|
| `https://studywithtymee.com` | **200** |
| `https://www.studywithtymee.com` | **200** (apex 로 301) |
| `https://api.studywithtymee.com/swagger-ui/` | **200** |
| `/api/v1/classroom` | **401** (인증 정상) |
| `/actuator/health` | **404** (의도대로 차단, #28) |

```
브라우저 --https--> Cloudflare --https(443)--> nginx --http(8080)--> Spring
```

## Let's Encrypt 가 아니라 Cloudflare Origin Certificate

브라우저가 검증하는 것은 **CF 의 인증서**고 원본 인증서는 CF 만 봅니다.
Origin Certificate 는 CF 가 자기 CA 로 발급하며 **15년짜리라 갱신 크론이 없습니다.**

그리고 Let's Encrypt 는 여기서 쓰기 까다롭습니다 — 암호화 모드가 `전체` 면
CF 가 원본 **443** 에 붙으므로, 원본에 인증서가 없으면 **HTTP-01 검증 요청조차 도달하지 못합니다.**

## `X-Forwarded-Proto` 에 `$scheme` 을 쓰지 않습니다

프록시 뒤에서 `$scheme` 은 **"CF → 원본" 구간의 프로토콜**이라 항상 `https` 입니다.
브라우저가 무엇으로 왔는지는 `CF-Visitor` 헤더에만 있습니다.
`$scheme` 을 쓰면 백엔드가 리다이렉트 URL·쿠키 secure 플래그를 잘못 정합니다.

## WebSocket 기본값 세 개

| 기본값 | 증상 |
|---|---|
| `proxy_http_version 1.0` | `Upgrade` 미전달 → 핸드셰이크 **400** |
| `proxy_read_timeout 60s` | **60초마다 끊긴다.** 에러 로그도 안 남는다 |
| `proxy_buffering on` | 프레임이 버퍼에 고여 지연 증가 |

## 겪은 것 세 가지

### ① `521 Web Server Is Down`

암호화 모드가 `전체` 라 **CF 가 원본 443 에 붙는데 원본은 80만 듣고** 있었습니다.
제가 예상한 닭-달걀이 그대로 나왔습니다.

### ② `unknown directive "http2"`

`http2 on;` 은 **nginx 1.25.1+** 문법인데 서버는 **1.20.1** 이었습니다.

> **`nginx -t` 가 잡아서 reload 가 거부됐고 기존 프로세스가 그대로 살았습니다.**
> 사이트가 더 나빠지지 않았습니다. 적용 전 문법 검사가 이래서 필요합니다.

### ③ `403 Permission denied` — SELinux

`getenforce` = **Enforcing**. `/var/www/edumeet` 이 `var_t` 라 nginx(`httpd_t`)가 못 읽습니다.

```
unconfined_u:object_r:var_t:s0              /var/www/edumeet      ← 막힘
system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0    /usr/share/nginx/html ← 정상
```

**파일 권한(`rw-r--r--`)은 멀쩡해서 `ls -l` 로는 절대 못 찾습니다.**

```bash
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/var/www/edumeet(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/edumeet
```

`chcon` 이 아니라 **규칙을 등록**해야 재라벨링 후에도 남습니다.

## 아직 안 한 것

- **8080 이 `0.0.0.0/0` 으로 열려 있습니다** (보안 목록 규칙 `kokjip`).
  원본 IP 로 백엔드에 직접 붙는 **우회로**입니다. nginx 가 섰으니 닫는 게 맞습니다
- 암호화 모드 `전체(엄격)` + Origin Certificate (지금은 자체서명 + `전체(비엄격)`)
- **WebSocket 이 프록시 뒤에서 실제로 유지되는지 측정**

body: A host editor finds the image someone is editing by **hit-testing the cursor** and walking the paint stack, not by reading `design.json` — so `pointer-events-none` on a media element makes it invisible to that test, and a decorative layer over one *without* it swallows the hover. Either way the "Change image" affordance never appears and a fully-propped image reads as uneditable, worst on the full-bleed heroes where the image *is* the section. Five sections were shaped that way: restaurant `Hero` + `Reservation`, `deck/ImageFull` and `agency/WorkGrid` had scrims that ate the pointer, and `annual-report/Cover` had the class on the `` itself, which is the worse half (a click can't reach it either). The rule now lives in `_base/AGENTS.md` and `CONTRACT.md`, and `check-media-editable.mjs` enforces both halves over `src/**/*.tsx` on every build — it runs on the *assembled* workspace beside `extract-design.mjs`, so it covers an AI-authored system as well as a shipped kit. It warns in a consumer's design turn (a class heuristic must never fail somebody's turn) and errors here, where CI sets `KOPLA_MEDIA_STRICT=1`. Also included: `@kind` now carries into an array's element type, so `@kind image` on `gallery: string[]` is no longer silently dropped. Rebased onto #30 — the two collide directly, and both bugs survived it: `Cover`'s `` lost `motion.img` but kept `pointer-events-none`, and `ImageFull`'s background became CSS parallax with its gradient still opaque to the pointer. Verified after the rebase: public-safety clean, all 13 kits build strict, components + demo build, and **every `design.json` is byte-identical to main** — including #30's slimmed `hydrateSections`, so this is behaviour-only. Confirmed the check still fails on all five bugs in their post-#30 shapes with correct line numbers. Pairs with vev-design/kopla#436, which fixes the host side (hover resolved from the paint stack, swaps actually persisted). Landing this one needs a `ref` bump in `apps/web/kits.config.json` afterwards. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: ferlzjordanx
body:
## Summary
w-9-2-planner P2, foundation slice only — no embeddings, retrieval interface, citations, or evaluation yet (those are separate later slices per `references/vector-rag.md`).

- **`libs/policy_corpus/manifest.py`**: loads `docs/RagDocs/manifest.json` and enforces its ingestion contract before any document body is read — absolute paths, traversal, symlink escape, unsupported extension, oversize file, duplicate `source_id`/version, missing file, and content hash mismatch are all hard structural errors (`ManifestValidationError`). A document that is merely not yet `synthetic`/`retrieval_enabled`/`approved_training` is excluded from the ingestable set, not an error for the whole manifest.
- **`libs/policy_corpus/chunking.py`**: deterministic Markdown heading-based chunker driven by the manifest's own character-based chunking config (`max_characters`/`overlap_characters`/`minimum_characters`), producing stable `source_id@source_version#section_id` chunk identity — same input always produces the same chunk ids/hashes.
- **`db/migrations/024_policy_corpus.sql`** (+ `db/schema.sql`): additive `policy_documents`/`policy_chunks` tables. Deliberately separate from `rag_embeddings` (patient-scoped, fixed `VECTOR(16)`) — no embedding column yet, added when a real embedding provider is selected in a later slice.

author: marianoalvarosaiz
body:
https://liferay.atlassian.net/browse/LPD-103440

## What Is Being Fixed

`com.liferay.portal.verify.test.PreupgradeVerifyDatabasePrivilegesTest#testVerifySelectRowPrivilege` failed on the `modules-integration-sqlserver2019` shard of `[master] ci:test:upgrade - 365 - 2026-08-23[18:46:00]`, commit `d53d6af13dbc77f2d808f9f92c65ed72bd643f85` (Testray case result 513667831).

```
testVerifySelectRowPrivilege: java.lang.AssertionError: Thread Thread[#73,PersistedQuartzSchedulerEngineInstance_QuartzSchedulerThread,5,QuartzScheduler:PersistedQuartzSchedulerEngineInstance] caught concurrent failure: java.lang.AssertionError: {level=ERROR, loggerName=org.quartz.core.ErrorLogger, message=An error occurred while scanning for the next triggers to fire.
	at com.liferay.portal.test.rule.LogAssertionTestRule$LogAppender.append(LogAssertionTestRule.java:318)
	at org.quartz.core.ErrorLogger.schedulerError(QuartzScheduler.java:2361)
	at org.quartz.core.QuartzSchedulerThread.run(QuartzSchedulerThread.java:271)
Caused by: org.quartz.JobPersistenceException: Couldn't acquire next trigger: The SELECT permission was denied on the object 'QUARTZ_TRIGGERS', database 'lportal', schema 'dbo'.
	at org.quartz.impl.jdbcjobstore.JobStoreSupport.acquireNextTrigger(JobStoreSupport.java:2827)
	at org.quartz.impl.jdbcjobstore.JobStoreSupport.acquireNextTriggers(JobStoreSupport.java:2751)
	at org.quartz.core.QuartzSchedulerThread.run(QuartzSchedulerThread.java:264)
```

There is no offending commit. The same commit passed on the other seven dialect shards, and the test has failed once in its last 290 recorded executions on this routine, so `lastPassSha` and `firstFailSha` are the same commit. This is a latent race in the test rather than a regression.

Every test method in the class revokes a privilege from a `test` database user and then installs a data source for that user through `InfrastructureUtil.setDataSource`, which is portal wide. `QuartzConnectionProvider.getConnection` resolves `InfrastructureUtil.getDataSource()` on every connection request rather than holding a reference, so the persisted scheduler thread picks the privilege starved data source up as soon as the swap happens. When its poll for the next trigger lands inside that window it hits the revoked privilege, Quartz reports the failure at `ERROR` through `org.quartz.core.ErrorLogger`, and `LogAssertionTestRule` turns that unexpected `ERROR` into a failure of whichever test method is running. Whether the poll lands inside the window is purely a matter of timing, which is why the failure is rare and not tied to a commit.

The same run also failed `PortalLogAssertorTest#testScanXMLLog`, which reports the very same Quartz `ERROR` again after it is written to the portal XML log.

This race was already diagnosed identically on LPD-87266 and its subtask LPD-91084 in May 2026, for `testVerifyDeleteRowPrivilege` plus the same `PortalLogAssertorTest` symptom. Both were closed as Discarded on 2026-06-16 with the comment "No longer reproducible" and the race was never addressed.

## How It Is Being Fixed

`setUp` silences the `org.quartz` logger for the lifetime of each test method and `tearDown` restores it, after the test data source has been destroyed and the test user dropped, so the whole window is covered including teardown, which is where LPD-87266's second symptom appeared. While the privilege is revoked the portal's scheduler cannot work by construction, so the errors it reports in that window are an expected consequence of the test rather than a product defect. This is the same mechanism the sibling `PreupgradeVerifyDatabaseStateTest` in this module already uses for expected errors.

Silencing the logger rather than filtering the captured message fixes both symptoms at once. `LoggerTestUtil.configureLog4JLogger` sets the level to `OFF` and turns additivity off, so the event is never emitted, never reaches the root appender that `LogAssertionTestRule` installs, and never reaches the portal XML log that `PortalLogAssertorTest` scans. `org.quartz` is the logger the portal itself already declares in `portal-log4j.xml`, so the capture restores it to exactly its previous level and additivity.

The assertions each test method makes about the verify process's privilege errors are untouched.

Verified locally on PostgreSQL, where `testVerifySelectRowPrivilege` is `Assume` skipped, using a temporary probe that logs the same `ERROR` from a background thread inside the swap window. Without the fix the probe reproduced the CI failure frame for frame; with the fix applied and the probe still present the test passed; and with the probe removed the committed state passed. The probe is not part of this change.

This pull request supersedes #3882, which carried the `LPD-103441` subtask key in its commit subject instead of the parent `LPD-103440`. The tree is identical.

## Why Are There No Tests?

The whole diff is test code and there is no product change to cover. The failure is a timing race that cannot be asserted deterministically without silencing the very logger the fix configures. The alternative, capturing at `ERROR` and asserting no unexpected message, would require enumerating every message Quartz emits when its database is unreachable, and any new benign message would fail the test, which trades this flake for a different one.

## PR Check

**pr-check: PASS** — tested on `c2d31e9ad115be9b69e1287ece659e311ede1752`, whose tree is byte identical to this PR's head `a3e9baebf4d2e1afe5b9a54d8a23f967030b5d36`. The only change is the commit subject's ticket key.

| Validation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Source Format | PASS |
| Transaction Usage | PASS |
| Per-Module Compile | PASS |
| Integration Test Compile | PASS |
| Baseline | PASS |
| Java Unit Tests | PASS |

author: thebenignhacker
body:
The 1.3.0 pre-tag release test found that every `aim-arp telemetry` subcommand executed when asked for help: the dispatcher chose what to run from the subcommand name alone and never validated the arguments, so `--help` rode along invisibly.

- `telemetry opt-out --help` performed a real opt-out — the marker was written by the question. `opt-in --help` removed one.
- On a machine that had sent, `purge --help` would have fired the right-to-delete from a help query.
- Unknown options were silently swallowed the same way (`status --bogus` ran status).

**Fix (first commit)**
- `--help` / `-h` anywhere in the arguments print usage and change nothing; help wins even alongside a recognized option.
- An unrecognized option is an error naming the option (exit 1) instead of a silent no-op. `opt-out --no-purge` keeps working.
- From the same release test (P2): `telemetry status` attributed `OPENA2A_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` and `ARP_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` to a bare "environment variable" with no clearing instruction, while `OPENA2A_TELEMETRY` already got "unset it to clear". All three now name their variable.

**Second commit — adversarial review of the first found the guard incomplete**
- `telemetry --help -x` (help in the subcommand slot plus junk) fell through to the unknown-option check and errored a help query that succeeded before; help in the subcommand slot now answers first.
- A mistyped subcommand with `--help` alongside exited 0, losing the typo signal; the subcommand is validated against `TELEMETRY_SUBCOMMANDS` before either shortcut, so `frobnicate --help` reports the typo.
- The internal CLI dispatched `register` before the shared guard, so `register --help` would have built and sent a real enrollment — the same class on the highest-side-effect subcommand. Guarded the same way. (Not a shipped-bin path; the npm package registers only `aim-arp`.)
- Attribution read raw env truthiness while `isOptedOut` reads strict truthiness, so `OPENA2A_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=0` alongside a marker blamed the variable with a clearing instruction that would clear nothing. `optOutReason` now reads the same `envTruthy` predicate as the decision.
- The help tests asserted only that nothing executed; help output is now asserted positively.

**Tests**: 17 regression tests in `telemetry-help-noexec.test.ts`; 11 fail against the pre-fix dispatcher and 6 against the first commit (the OPTOUT=0 attribution test fails against both; the one remaining is the existing-behavior control for `--no-purge`). Full suite 1153 green.

Blocks the `sdk-ts-v1.3.0` tag until merged. Remaining release-test P3s are filed on #412.

author: frikkern
body:
## Premise correction first

This lane was dispatched to fix gh-8463 ("Studio cannot browse consumer-registered types") on the belief it was still live. **It is not.** #8463 was fixed by #8471, merged `eb23ef9544` on 2026-08-02. The hardcoded `Map.has_key?(schemas, "post")` list is real but is only the *curated* group; `build_generic_types_group/2` has caught everything else since that PR. Verified by mutation: reverting that fix reds the `issue #8463` tests at `structure_test.exs:235` and `:264`.

What IS still broken is the adjacent case, and it is worse.

## The defect

`SchemaDefinition.visibility` defaults to `"public"`, and `SchemaController.upsert/2` passes attrs straight through with no default injected. So a consumer POSTing to `/v1/schemas/:dataset` **without** a `visibility` key gets `"public"`.

Both desk catch-alls filtered on `visibility == "private"`, and the curated content group hardcodes post/page/project. So a public consumer type matched **nothing**. `…Rest` is census-driven (`Analytics.type_census/2`), so with zero documents it appeared **nowhere in the desk at all**.

Probed on the unfixed tree (`origin/main` d4d228c132):

| case | result before |
|---|---|
| public, 0 docs | `type_names: []` — invisible |
| public, 1 doc | only `rest-recipe` under `…Rest` |
| public, `singleton: true` | settings node `nil`, `type_names: []` — **vanished, flag ignored** |
| private control | lands in `content-types` correctly |

This is Gyldendal field-report finding **#25**, already diagnosed in `task-6bfcb72042178fd0` (S8), unclaimed: *"singleton:true is ignored for public schemas; types with no documents are invisible until the Rest tier surfaces them... private-vs-public is doing double duty as both an access control and a desk-curation control, and those two jobs need separating."*

## Options enumerated, and why this one

`visibility` is an **access** control. `api/CLAUDE.md` states it plainly: `"public"` = anonymous reads, `"private"` = 404 on the public API, token required. Using it to *also* decide desk curation is the bug.

1. **Default new schemas to `visibility: "private"` at the controller.** Rejected — changes an *access* default (security-relevant) to fix a display bug, and breaks every consumer relying on public reads.
2. **Add the `deskSection` key now.** This is #25's stated fix and remains the right end state, but it answers *which section* — strictly larger than *does the type appear at all*. Left to the S8 parent; noted below so it is not lost.
3. **Fall back to census when a schema has no documents.** Rejected — a heuristic, and it re-guesses the same question every future reader has to re-derive.
4. **Chosen: remove the coupling.** Desk placement keys on `singleton` **alone** — the explicit declaration that already exists, added by #8471. No new field, no guess-from-shape rule. Curated groups now run first and hand their claimed type names to both catch-alls, so a curated public type (`paper`, `post`) is never *also* dumped into the generic bucket.

This makes the code match the invariant its own moduledoc already claimed: *"a schema is drillable list (Content) XOR singleton (Settings), never both, never neither."* That was false for every public schema.

## Callers enumerated

`git grep` over `api/lib` + `api/test`:

- `structure.ex` — `build_desk_items/3` composition; `collect_claimed_types` feeding the `…Rest` exclusion
- `structure_controller.ex` moduledoc; `frt.ex` comment; `schema_definition.ex` comment — all three stated the old private-only law and are corrected here
- `structure_test.exs` `content_types_node` helper; `structure_clean_desk_test.exs` `@host_node_ids`
- Go TUI consumes the tree over `GET /v1/structure/:dataset` and switches on node `type`. **No new node `type` is introduced**, so old binaries render this unchanged. No response-shape change, so no OpenAPI regen.

## Second-order effects, named

- Types that previously surfaced **only** under `…Rest` move up into `Content`; `…Rest` shrinks. Pinned by a test.
- A public schema with `singleton: true` now renders as a `:document` node whose id equals the type name — the singleton pane contract. Correct, because the schema explicitly asked for it, but it **is** a render change for anyone who set the flag on a public schema and had it silently ignored.
- `Node.visibility` is still hardcoded `:public` by `doc_type_list_item/1`. It has **no reader** anywhere in `lib/` (`scope_plugin_nodes/4` gates on `requires_type`, not this field), so it is inert. Left alone rather than widened here; worth a separate look.

## An existing test was a spec

`structure_test.exs` had *"an empty private set produces neither a Settings nor a Content group"*. It still passes, but for a different reason — `post` is *curated*, not merely public. Renamed and commented so the rationale does not silently rot into a false green.

## Proof

Five new tests. **Three are mutation-proved fix-dependent** — reverting `structure.ex` to base reds exactly:

```
1) ...a PUBLIC consumer type with zero documents gets a browsable Content row
2) ...a type that moved into Content is claimed, so it leaves …Rest
3) ...a PUBLIC schema with singleton: true reaches Settings instead of vanishing
32 tests, 3 failures
```

Restoring returns them to green. The other two are regression guards that correctly pass both before and after (curated types must not double-list; private types still reach Content).

**50 tests, 0 failures** across `structure_test`, `structure_clean_desk_test`, `structure_media_test`, `structure_plugin_struct_gating_test`, `structure_tasks_desk_test`, `structure_workspace_scope_test`, `structure_controller_test` — re-run after rebase onto `origin/main`.

Wider sweep of `test/barkpark_web/studio/` was 394 tests, 1 failure in `claude_chat_cloud_session_test.exs` — a subprocess argv-capture test that fails on a different case run-to-run, contains zero references to `Structure`/`PaneBuilder`/`schema`, and names no file this diff touches. Pre-existing and environmental, not mine.

## Not in scope

`deskSection` — letting a consumer choose *which* section its type lands in — remains unbuilt and stays with the S8 parent row `task-6bfcb72042178fd0`.

Separately, gh-8463 is **still open** with the reporter never told the fix shipped 22 days ago; filed as `task-3044ea0939fb056b`.

author: leiicamundi
body:
## The bug

`scripts/run-terraform-test-touched.sh` is a `pre-commit` hook entry, so it runs
on contributor machines, not only on CI runners. It used two bash 4 features:

- `mapfile -t STAGED < <(...)`
- `declare -A TEST_DIRS`

macOS still ships bash 3.2.57 as `/bin/bash` — the last GPLv2 release, frozen in
2007 — and has neither. On any Mac without a newer bash earlier in `PATH`, the
hook dies immediately:

```
scripts/run-terraform-test-touched.sh: line 23: mapfile: command not found
```

Exit 127, so `pre-commit run --all-files` fails on **every branch**, including a
pristine `main`. `AGENTS.md` tells contributors to run exactly that command after
every change, which means the instruction cannot be followed on a stock Mac. CI
runs Linux with bash 5 and never saw it.

## The fix

Drop the arrays. Staged paths and resolved test directories are newline-delimited
strings, deduplicated with `sort -u` instead of associative-array keys, and both
loops are fed by here-strings rather than pipes so the `fail` flag survives into
the final `exit`.

Behaviour is unchanged: same directories selected, same dedup, same exit codes.
The rewrite is also slightly shorter than what it replaces.

A comment now records the constraint, so the next edit does not reintroduce a
bash 4 builtin.

## Verification

A throwaway harness with a stubbed `terraform` covered six cases against both
shells — bash 3.2.57 (macOS `/bin/bash`) and bash 5.2.26 (Linux container),
6/6 on each:

| case | expected |
|---|---|
| nothing staged | exit 0, no output |
| one staged `.tf` under a dir with `tests/` | that dir runs |
| two staged files in the same dir | exactly one run (dedup holds) |
| staged files in two dirs | both run |
| `terraform test` fails | exit 1 and a `FAILED` line |
| staged `.tf` with no `tests/` above it | exit 0, no output |

`pre-commit run --all-files` is now green end to end on macOS, including the
`Terraform test (touched states)` hook that used to abort.

## Notes for the reviewer

- One file, +20/−9, no behaviour change and no workflow touched.
- `generic/openshift/dual-region/procedure/check-deployment-ready.sh` also uses
  `declare -A`, and is deliberately left alone: it already detects old bash and
  fails fast with a clear message, and it is a user-facing procedure where
  requiring bash 4 is a documented prerequisite rather than a silent hook abort.
- Installing a newer bash (`brew install bash`) also works around this locally,
  but the hook should not require it.

author: cevheri
body:
fix(agent): the model sweep reported a pass it had not measured, and a table nobody had re-measured

Three defects in what produces and publishes the model figures. They share a shape: the tool
reported something other than what happened, and nothing was watching.

THE SWEEP'S EXIT STATUS WAS SED'S. Playwright was piped through `sed` to prefix each line
with the model's name, so `$?` belonged to sed, which always succeeds — and there was no
`set -e` and no `pipefail`. A model could fail its entire UI sweep while the script printed
`done` and exited 0, so anything reading that status was told a sweep passed that had not.

`${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is now read immediately after the pipeline. Failures are COLLECTED across
the loop rather than exited on — an hour of measurement is worth finishing, and one model
failing is not a reason to stop asking about the other nine — then named and the script exits
non-zero. The `sed` prefix stays: the pipe was never the problem, not reading past it was.

VIDEO WAS DELETED FOR EXACTLY THE RUNS THE SWEEP EXISTS TO PRODUCE. The comment said videos
are kept "for every test rather than only for failures, because the agent specs are the ones
somebody watches", and the value beneath it was `retain-on-failure`, which deletes the video
of every passing test. Now `on` when `AGENT_MODEL_E2E` is set and `retain-on-failure`
otherwise — scoped rather than global, because `use` reaches every project and `on` there
would have CI keep a video of every passing test in every job.

AND `docs/AGENT.md` PUBLISHED A SECOND, STALE COPY OF THE MEASUREMENTS. Ten links into a
`docs/models/` directory that does not exist, and — this is beyond what the review that raised
it claimed — ALL TEN ROWS disagreeing with the canonical table in `docs/llms/README.md`, in
both directions and by wide margins: `gemma4:26b` published 46 s/180 s against a measured
36 s/92 s, `qwen3:14b` 39 s/151 s against 41 s/303 s.

Aligning the numbers was the obvious fix and is the wrong one. The defect is not that a figure
was wrong, it is that one measurement had two homes — which is what produced the drift and
would produce it again. So the copy is gone and the section points at the canonical table,
saying plainly what was removed and why, with two of the drifted figures named so the next
person can tell this was a duplicate rather than a deletion of something.

A test guards both tools, because both defects are the kind that return quietly. It asserts
the properties that actually break rather than the presence of a word: the ADJACENCY of the
status read — `PIPESTATUS` holds the last pipeline's statuses and any command in between
replaces it, so an `echo` inserted there restores the original bug — and the CONDITION on the
video setting, together with the fact that the variable it keys on is one the sweep really
sets. Verified by mutation: inserting a line between the pipeline and the read turns it red.

Verified: format, lint (0 errors), typecheck, knip, `bun run test` (33/33 groups), build,
`bash -n` on the script, and coverage:check at 42537/42537 lines.

author: samuelmolero26
body:
## What

Raises the release binary size gate from 20 MB to 32 MB, and records in a comment both what the gate is for and why the headroom is sized the way it is.

## Why

The 20 MB cap predates the tree-sitter mapper tier and was never revisited. **Every platform is over it today, so any tag cut from `develop` fails the release job.**

Measured by building the commit before `gotreesitter` entered `go.mod` (parent of #112, `6ceb091`) in a throwaway worktree, using the exact flags from `release.yml` — `-trimpath -ldflags "-s -w"` plus the four `grammar_subset_*` tags:

| linux/amd64 | bytes |
|---|---|
| before the mapper (`6ceb091`) | 17,936,546 |
| `develop` today (`90e64e9`) | 24,686,754 |
| **delta** | **+6,750,208 (+38%)** |
| current cap | 20,971,520 |

## This was not accepted on trust — the alternative was measured and rejected

Before raising the number, I looked for the bloat directly. Attribution via `gsa` (includes metadata, not just text):

| | size | % |
|---|---|---|
| gotreesitter | 5.3 MB | 21.3% |
| modernc.org/sqlite | 3.4 MB | 13.7% |
| crypto | 1.5 MB | 5.9% |
| net | 1.3 MB | 5.1% |
| x/tools + go/types + go/parser | 2.0 MB | 7.9% |
| **droids-mem's own code** | **669 kB** | **2.7%** |

Roughly half the binary is Go metadata no dependency owns — `pclntab` 6.65 MB plus `typerel`/`_type`/`go:func`/`go:string` 6.14 MB, 52% of a 24.66 MB on-disk symbol total.

**Three candidate cuts were investigated and all three are being declined:**

1. **Dropping unused-language normalization from gotreesitter — prototyped, works, rejected.** The `grammar_subset_*` tags gate grammar *blobs*, not the hand-written per-language normalization code in the 77 untagged `parser_result_*.go` files, which stays reachable through a live `switch lang.Name`. I built a patched module (63 files deleted, 33 dispatch arms removed) and measured **24,686,754 → 23,236,770, saving 1,449,984 bytes** with `go test ./...` green and TS/Python parsing verified end to end. Declined deliberately: more languages are planned, and this code is what those languages will need. Also worth recording — the patch cascaded, restoring 34 of 63 files, because general helpers live in language-named files (`parser_result_go.go` defines `shiftNodeBytes` and `flattenRootSelfFragments`, used from `glr_forest.go` and `injection.go`).

2. **`net/http/httptest` reaching production via mcp-go.** Real defect — `server/sse.go:9` and `server/streamable_http.go:13` import a test-only stdlib package to export test helpers. Measured at **4,096 bytes**, because `net/http` imports `crypto/tls` unconditionally and httptest was never the cause of the crypto weight. Reported upstream as hygiene, not as a size fix: mark3labs/mcp-go#961.

3. **`crypto` at 1.5 MB in a loopback-only tool.** Traced to `net/http`'s unconditional `crypto/tls` import — x509, ASN.1, nistec curves, ML-KEM. Not removable without hand-rolling HTTP on an auth-bearing surface. Not worth it.

Also checked and clean: no tracked binaries linked into the build, 10 direct dependencies with no duplication, 33 kB of embedded fixtures, and first-party code at 205 kB graph / 145 store / 130 tui / 105 mcpserver.

## Why 32 specifically

The gate's real job is catching a build that lost the `grammar_subset_*` tags and embedded all 206 grammars. That build is **41,959,314 bytes** and still fails loudly at 32 MB.

The headroom is sized for the language roadmap. Since every language's normalization code is already linked regardless of tags, adding a language costs only its grammar blob — about **91 kB** averaged over the 202 the subset tags exclude (41,959,314 − 23,644,898, over 202). 32 MB leaves room for a large number of additional languages before this gate is worth revisiting.

## Note for anyone re-measuring

`go tool nm -size` sorted by size puts `crypto/internal/fips140/drbg.memory` on top at 33,554,432 bytes — larger than the whole binary. It is a `__noptrbss` zerofill buffer occupying **zero** file bytes (`size -m` labels it "(zerofill)"). Filter out `B`/`b` symbols before ranking anything. Runtime is unaffected: 5 live server processes measured 30.2 MB RSS combined.

## Checklist

- [x] **Changelog**: not added — CI-only change, no user-facing behavior changed
- [x] **Tests**: no code changed; `go test -race -shuffle=on ./...` passes (9 packages, exit 0)
- [x] **Lint**: `golangci-lint run --timeout 5m` reports `0 issues.`
- [x] **Dependencies**: no go.mod/go.sum changes
- [x] **Commit**: conventional

Three follow-up fixes from real testing of the overlay pin-capture feature:

- computeOverlay() resized #pdf-canvas to the preview images' dimensions but never resynced #markup-svg's viewBox, so the pin tool's drag-to-canvas coordinate math sampled outside the actual canvas bounds and captured nothing. Now synced on every recompute.

author: alrobbertz
body:
### Problem: swxsoc gets "stuck" on the wrong mission depending on import order

`padre_meddea` (like the other affiliated instrument packages) sets the `SWXSOC_MISSION` environment variable at import time so that `swxsoc` loads the correct mission configuration. However, the old logic only set the variable *if it wasn't already set*, and never told `swxsoc` to reload its config:

```python
SWXSOC_MISSION = os.getenv("SWXSOC_MISSION", "padre")
os.environ["SWXSOC_MISSION"] = SWXSOC_MISSION

from swxsoc import config as swxsoc_config
from swxsoc import log as swxsoc_log
```

If `swxsoc` happened to get imported *before* `padre_meddea` (e.g. by another dependency, a notebook cell, or a test fixture), `swxsoc` had already loaded its default (`demo`) mission config the first time it was imported. Importing `padre_meddea` afterward did correctly set `os.environ["SWXSOC_MISSION"] = "padre"`, but since Python caches imported modules, `from swxsoc import config as swxsoc_config` just grabbed the **stale, already-loaded `demo` config** — `swxsoc.config["mission"]["mission_name"]` stayed `"demo"` even though the env var itself was correct.

**Before (broken):**
```python
>>> import swxsoc
>>> swxsoc.config["mission"]["mission_name"]
'demo'
>>> import padre_meddea
>>> swxsoc.config["mission"]["mission_name"]
'demo'          # still wrong, even though padre_meddea "set" SWXSOC_MISSION
```

### Solution

`padre_meddea/__init__.py` now unconditionally forces its own mission and explicitly calls `swxsoc.reconfigure()` to force a fresh reload of `swxsoc`'s config, regardless of what happened before it was imported:

`config`/`log` are now fetched from `swxsoc` **after** the forced reconfigure, so `padre_meddea.config` is guaranteed to reflect the `padre` mission no matter the import order.

### Example now fixed

```python
>>> import swxsoc
>>> swxsoc.config["mission"]["mission_name"]
'demo'
>>> import padre_meddea
>>> swxsoc.config["mission"]["mission_name"]
'padre'          # ✅ correctly reconfigured
```

author: raigfp
body:
## Problem

A `repos.txt` saved with Windows line endings (CRLF) breaks `fetch`: the all-git fast path hands the file to `fetch_bundles.sh` byte-for-byte, `read` keeps the trailing `\r` on every line, and git fails with:

```
fatal: unable to access 'https://gitlab.example.com/group/repo.git?/': URL rejected: Malformed input to a URL function
```

The `?/` is misleading: git prints the invisible `\r` as `?` and appends `/` itself in the error message, so it looks like the tool corrupted a valid URL. Hit by a partner running the CLI on a repos list edited on Windows.

## Fix

- `_partition_urls` reads the file as bytes (universal-newline decoding hides the `\r`) and treats CR anywhere in the file — or stray whitespace around a URL — as a reason to write a normalized temp file for the bash script instead of passing the original.
- `fetch_bundles.sh` also strips a trailing `\r` per line, so standalone use with a CRLF file works too.

## Tests

Added CRLF and padded-URL cases to `tests/test_fetch_partition.py`; full suite passes (401).

author: allidoizcode
body:
Closes #1131. Finishes #975's "record" half, which #976 could only close for the two hosts it recognises.

## The gap

#976 refuses a Solana claim declaring a cluster other than the node's own — but only when the node knows its own. That comes from `SolanaSettlementConfig::cluster_hint`, a **five-host allowlist** over `[settlement.solana] rpc_url`. Everything else answers `None`, and `None` switches the check off entirely.

| Node shape | `cluster_hint` | Checked before this PR? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `infra/linode-{relay,store}` (`api.devnet.solana.com`) | `devnet` | yes |
| Helius / Alchemy / QuickNode / Triton | `None` | **no** |
| private RPC, IP literal, SSH tunnel, caching proxy | `None` | **no** |
| all three `local/` topologies (`http://solana-validator:8899`) | `None` | **no** |

A paid provider is the ordinary production shape, and it is where the value at risk is highest — the mainnet node is the one whose claims are worth mislabelling. The allowlist cannot be grown to reach it: provider hostnames are not enumerable, and a substring match on "mainnet" is a false-positive machine.

## The fix

A cluster's genesis hash is the identity the chain states about *itself*, so it holds however the node reached the chain. `SolanaSettlementBackend::connect` now reads `getGenesisHash` alongside the four identity reads it already makes, and `cluster()` carries the answer through `Runtime` to the client edge.

The three published values are **not written down** — they come from `solana_sdk::genesis_config::ClusterType::get_genesis_hash()` in the `=2.1.0` SDK already pinned here, so they track the dependency. One unit test pins that table to the base58 the endpoints answer with:

| Cluster | Genesis hash |
| --- | --- |
| mainnet-beta | `5eykt4UsFv8P8NJdTREpY1vzqKqZKvdpKuc147dw2N9d` |
| devnet | `EtWTRABZaYq6iMfeYKouRu166VU2xqa1wcaWoxPkrZBG` |
| testnet | `4uhcVJyU9pJkvQyS88uRDiswHXSCkY3zQawwpjk2NsNY` |

Verified two ways that agree exactly: the pinned SDK's own table, and `getGenesisHash` against `api.{mainnet-beta,devnet,testnet}.solana.com` on 2026-08-24. An SDK bump that moved one now fails the gate rather than silently relabelling a chain.

## The local topologies are unaffected, on purpose

`solana-test-validator` mints a fresh genesis every run and its `ClusterType::Development` has no published hash — it can never match one. An unrecognised genesis therefore means *"this node cannot name its cluster"*, exactly what `cluster_hint`'s `None` already means, and never "refuse". `a_test_validators_fresh_genesis_names_no_cluster_and_still_connects` asserts both halves against a real spawned validator: `connect` succeeds, `cluster()` is `None`. All three `local/` topologies keep the behaviour they had before this PR (no check), and the same `solana-test-validator` image serves `getGenesisHash` fine.

## Fail-closed at boot, and why that is not a new decision

`connect` already makes four RPC round trips before the node serves anything — two `get_account`s, a **submitted** transaction (`ensure_own_ata_exists`) and a `simulate_transaction` — and each refuses startup on failure; `connect_refuses_an_unreachable_rpc_endpoint` asserts it. A node with `[settlement.solana]` configured **already does not boot when its RPC is unreachable**. A fifth read changes no outage surface: if it fails, the four ahead of it already have.

The one genuinely new call is what to do when the hint and the chain disagree (`mainnet.helius-rpc.com` answering devnet's genesis, say). This PR **takes the chain, logs a `warn`, and does not refuse** — refusing to boot because a hostname guess disagrees with a reading that has already superseded it would be an outage caused by the weaker source.

## Supersede, not replace

```
cluster = chain_genesis_hash.or(rpc_url_hostname_hint)
```

The hint stays as fallback because it covers the one case the chain cannot: a loopback test validator, unnameable by genesis but still `localnet` by URL. Deleting it would lose that for nothing; keeping it first would keep the bug.

**No config key is added.** Both sides derive from the `rpc_url` already there — one by reading it, one by dialling it — so this is **not a breaking deploy**, and no committed box TOML changes.

## Scope

Deliberately untouched: the claim-gate check itself, the `programId` wire contract (#1127), the peer-channel `program_id` declaration (#1128). `vectors/`, `local/`, `infra/`, the peer transports and `docs/protocol/` are all unchanged. The `runtime.rs` edit is one new `Runtime` field, one parameter threaded through two functions, and one new test.

## Gate

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cargo build --workspace` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --exclude payment-channel` — **1620 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored**, including the anvil- and validator-backed suites at real durations (`connect_identity` 5 passed in 27.00s)
- `cargo clippy --workspace --exclude payment-channel --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean

## Break-test

Dropping the chain value (`solana_cluster.or(cluster_hint)` → `cluster_hint`):

```
test runtime::tests::a_node_behind_a_paid_rpc_provider_still_checks_the_declared_cluster ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed: a node whose chain reports devnet must not endorse a claim
labelled mainnet-beta, even though its rpc_url's hostname names no cluster
  left: Ok(Solana(SolanaClientClaim { ... cluster: Some("mainnet-beta") }))
 right: Err(SolanaClusterMismatch { declared: "mainnet-beta", configured: "devnet" })
```

That `Ok(...)` is the pre-fix behaviour verbatim: the mislabelled claim accepted in full.

Making the mapping guess instead of answering `None` (`.or(Some("mainnet-beta"))`):

```
test cluster_identity_tests::a_genesis_hash_no_public_cluster_published_names_no_cluster ... FAILED
  left: Some("mainnet-beta")   right: None

test a_test_validators_fresh_genesis_names_no_cluster_and_still_connects ... FAILED
assertion failed: a fresh test-validator genesis matches no published cluster hash, so this node
must record that it cannot name its cluster rather than guess one
  left: Some("mainnet-beta")   right: None
```

Both restored; the gate above is the restored tree.

author: zakkaus
body:
`vm-zfs-encrypted` stalled twice at `MARK_24_DONE` with its console silent and `cpu 0.00`, and it is a `dist-bin` kernel with the official binary host on and no desktop — every test `_compiles()` applies says it is light, so it was given two cores and four gibibytes.

Its own `install.jsonl` says otherwise: nineteen packages compiled, among them `sys-fs/zfs`, `sys-boot/zfsbootmenu` with `fzf`, `kexec-tools` and `mbuffer`, `gentoo-kernel-bin`, `pahole`, `linux-firmware`, and `sys-apps/systemd` — the package it stopped inside both times. A binary kernel does not spare a ZFS layout, because the module is built against whatever kernel was installed and no binary host carries one.

Four fixtures move from light to heavy; the two ZFSBootMenu ones were already heavy through their desktop. `test_a_guest_that_compiles_is_given_a_whole_node` used `vm-zfs` as one of its two light examples, so it went red — the example was wrong rather than the assertion, and `vm-zfs` now stands in its heavy list with the reason beside it.
